behavior: AC1 — `recipient:` parses on a file-authority secret, is rejected on any other backend, and a secret without it verifies exactly as it does today.
evidence: 3 cases pass. Rejection on another backend and on a non-`age1` string are both asserted, the second because a private key pasted there by accident would commit the secret this file exists to protect. Undeclared is a deliberate no-op, asserted by checking the derive seam is never CALLED — not merely that the result is nil.

behavior: AC2 — verify reports FAILED when the derived recipient differs from the declared one, naming both.
evidence: Observed live against a scratch registry pointing at the REAL key with a deliberately wrong declaration, mutation confirmed distinct first: `FAILED ... derives recipient age166v8... but the registry declares age1qqq... — the key on this disk is not the declared one`, and the same registry with the right value returns `1 ok`. Unit case additionally pins that BOTH strings appear, because "they differ" without saying how sends the reader to the wrong one. Mutation: with the comparison replaced by a no-op (confirmed present, 0 matching lines) TestDrift_MismatchFailsAndNamesBoth FAILS; passes after revert.

behavior: AC3 — a check that cannot run reports its own failure rather than passing, and the pre-existing 34 entries do not regress.
evidence: `dotf secrets verify` -> 34 ok, 0 missing, 0 failed with the recipient declared on the live registry. The cannot-derive case asserts the underlying cause is carried, not swallowed: returning nil there would turn "age-keygen is absent" into "the key is fine", which is this check's own failure arriving through the check itself.

behavior: AC4 — backup writes escrow-manifest.json beside the escrow, un-ignored by exact name.
AC5 — the freshness check reports addition, modification and deletion distinctly, including a deletion whose survivors all predate the escrow.
AC6 — an escrow with no manifest is SKIPPED with the remediation named, never FAILED; no session is SKIPPED with a reason, never OK.
AC7 — the runbook names where the offline copy lives, and never its value.
evidence: The RECOVER protocol already named the location (an encrypted VeraCrypt USB) — #1000's AC1 was written when that was believed absent and was already half-satisfied. What was missing is the loop closing: step 1 now verifies the restored key against the declared recipient BEFORE the chain continues. A wrong key decrypts nothing and finds out four steps later; one from a stale backup decrypts SOME things, which is worse.

behavior: AC8 — GOOS=windows go vet clean, and any property not applicable on a platform says so in its own file.
verification: cd cli && go vet ./... && GOOS=windows go vet ./...
evidence: Both clean. Nothing in this slice touches a platform-specific property: deriving an age recipient and comparing two strings are portable, so no new build-tagged split was needed.
